newsitem.title: UK: Global LPG soft, but big backwardation looms.
newsitem.headline: Global LPG soft, but big backwardation looms.

text.p: International Liquefied Petroleum Gas (LPG) markets were quiet and weaker over the week in an uneasy standoff, with many anticipating a major price fall as the northern hemisphere winter eases.

In Europe and the Far East, buyers have been holding back in anticipation of weaker prices next month. And in the United States, retailers and dealers have been drawing down inventories rather than buying in new stocks, taking the view that the worst of the winter is already over.
The standoff in the Far East is based on uncertainty over the level of the Saudi Contract Price (CP) for February.

The CP is the benchmark against which most LPG east of the Middle East Gulf is traded, and spot tenders for cargoes lifting in the next forward month often give an indication of where the CP will be set.
The first February tender, or T1, was thought awarded at a little above $335 a tonne fob Gulf for both propane and butane.

The second, T2 tender, was rumoured done at well above $350, and possibly as high as $358, for propane while the butane price was thought much lower, close to $300. The T3 tender closes on Friday, and rumours on the award are expected to hit the market on Tuesday, just a few days before the February CP is announced.

The T2 award implies that there is still strength in the propane market, although most now expect the butane CP to fall. East Asian buying interest has fallen away because of the uncertainty, and in expectation that prices must start to fall as winter recedes.

"Stock levels (in Japan) are critically low, but everyone wants to push back their purchases as late as possible because of the price", said a Japanese trader. "If they can, they will try to survive until the end of March."
One dealer reported that a propane cargo for mid-February arrival traded recently at January CP + $29 a tonne C+F Japan.

Chinese demand has also stagnated, despite the demand spike caused by the Lunar New Year at the beginning of February. Requirements are being met out of storage, dealers said, with buyers preferring to restock later in the year rather than bringing in new supplies now.

"They're waiting for the T3 result," said a dealer. "If the butane CP comes down, they'll wait until next month before buying. But if it stays the same, they'll wait until March. If I was them, I'd wait until March."
While East Asia has stagnated, Europe has also been quiet, with many in the propane market anticipating a price collapse.

Large propane cargoes in Northwest Europe (NWE) are still valued above $400 a tonne cif NWE on a very prompt basis. But swaps -- often a good indicator of physical prices -- are valued at around $350 for the whole of February, and well below $300 for March. This implies a backwardation of around $100 during February, from $400 now to around $300 by the end of the month.

As a result, trade has slowed down as buyers are unwilling to commit themselves unless they need material immediately. "If you need it now, you need it now, but there are really no buyers," said a trader.

Small seagoing coasters in NWE are also quiet for the same reason, although sellers are more optimistic on that market. There are forecasts for a return of cold weather to Europe in early February, and sellers are confident that current price levels of around $435/$440 can be maintained in the short term.
"It's totally quiet," said one. "Sellers are waiting for the cold and buyers are waiting for a tumble, so there's a standstill. But I'm confident trade will be done at these levels next week."

The same fundamentals apply to propane in the Mediterranean as in NWE. Propane on a cif Lavera basis is discussed at around $370/$380 a tonne, although it was reported that a small 4,000 tonne ship was sold into Spain at $440 cif Spanish Mediterranean during the week.

Although in theory there is a sufficient price differential between the north and the Mediterranean to make movement of cargoes a possibility, in practice the lack of buyers in the north rules it out, dealers said. But there is still demand from Spain and Italy, and prices are expected to stay firm if the February CP stays at the same level.

Butane in the Mediterranean is currently priced at a differential to the NWE price, an indication of the lack of local interest. With a cif NWE price of around $240, dealers are adding $30 freight to come up with a notional $270 cif Lavera, but the market has been slow.

In the U.S., mild weather and lack of buying interest kept propane prices stable for much of the week, with spot prices at Mont Belvieu, Texas hovering at or slightly below 45.00 cents a gallon for the whole week.

Official data from the Department of Energy's Energy Information Administration showed a stockdraw of 2.7 million barrels of propane between January 10 and 17, and even though the industry had expected a stockdraw, the market remained stable in the belief that current stock levels are sufficient.
-- Sebastian Alison, London Newsroom +44 171 542 6412
